articles.headlineTranslated: Yokohama City University Identifies Nectin-4 as the Major Entry Receptor for Rubella Virus.
articles.summary: Rubella virus uses Nectin-4 as the major host cell entry receptor, a finding by a Yokohama City University–led team published in Nature (November 2026). Using rubella virus–like particles and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screens, they show Nectin-4 mediates entry in airway epithelial cells and placental syncytiotrophoblasts. In air–liquid interface airway models, rubella infects from the basal surface and releases progeny apically; infection is markedly reduced by Nectin-4 inhibition. Placental organoids reveal high Nectin-4 on syncytiotrophoblast surfaces, with infection suppressed by Nectin-4–blocking antibodies. Notably, Nectin-4 is also a measles virus receptor, suggesting shared host factors across these distinct viruses. This discovery advances understanding of rubella airway shedding and maternal–fetal transmission and may inform antiviral or vaccine strategies against congenital rubella syndrome. Background: global congenital rubella cases around 30,000/year (2019).

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles infection in a woman in the prefecture; possible contact with an unspecified number of people at a facility in Matsuyama City.
articles.summary: Measles infection has been confirmed in a woman in her 50s in Ehime Prefecture, with possible exposure to an unspecified number of people at two Matsuyama City facilities during the infectious period. As of Oct 23, this is the prefecture's third confirmed measles case this year. Two exposure sites: Sogo Mart Uemoto Store (Kita-Uemoto-cho) in Matsuyama City, on Oct 19 from 5:00–5:20 pm; and Supermarket Nitto Kume Store (Minami-Kume-cho) on Oct 21 from 9:05–9:15 am. The article notes airborne measles virus can survive less than two hours. The woman had visited the same location as a man in his 30s confirmed infected in Matsuyama City on Oct 10. Measles is highly contagious, and infection can occur in those without immunity after exposure. The health department is advising customers who may have visited the sites during those times to monitor for symptoms and seek guidance.

articles.headlineTranslated: A woman in her 50s contracted measles; Ehime Prefecture warns after she used two supermarkets.
articles.summary: Measles confirmed in Ehime Prefecture: A woman in her 50s living in the Chūyō Health Center jurisdiction has tested positive, marking Ehime’s third measles case this year. Illness began with fever, sore throat and a rash around Oct 20; she sought care in Matsuyama on Oct 22, with genetic testing confirming measles on Oct 23. She had one prior measles vaccination and no overseas travel history. She visited two Matsuyama supermarkets on Oct 19 and Oct 21, prompting the prefecture to advise customers who shopped there on those dates to monitor for symptoms. Nationwide, measles cases reached 579 this year. The article does not specify an infection source and does not indicate importation/exportation details.

articles.headlineTranslated: Trump administration cabinet members waving the anti-vaccine flag; measles surge in the United States, Japan also affected — Asahi Shimbun
articles.summary: Measles infections in the United States exceed 4,000 as of October 2026, the largest surge since elimination was declared in 2000. The outbreak correlates with declining preschool MMR vaccination coverage; 95% is the threshold to halt transmission, yet the 2025–26 kindergarten-entry MMR rate fell to 92.4% from 95.2% in 2019–20, with states below 90% increasing from 3 to 18. CDC data indicate about 95% of confirmed cases in 2025–26 occurred in unvaccinated individuals or those with unknown vaccination status. The WHO is poised to re‑evaluate elimination status this autumn, potentially overturning it. Commentary from Penn Medicine Lancaster General Hospital cites vaccine hesitancy amid public-health policy debates during the Trump era, with attribution to anti‑vaccine advocates such as Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The article also notes that Japan is affected amid global travel.

articles.headline: はしか患者が増加、強い感染力　症状は？ワクチンは？何が問題なのか：朝日新聞
articles.headlineTranslated: Measles cases rising, highly contagious: What are the symptoms? What about the vaccine? What is the problem? Asahi Shimbun
articles.summary: Measles is a highly contagious viral infection. In historical Japan, it was viewed as life-and-death, and in developing countries its case fatality has been cited at about 5–6%. After a roughly 10-day incubation, initial symptoms resemble a cold—fever, cough, and runny nose—followed by a high fever (above 39°C) and a spreading rash after 2–3 days, with the fever lasting several days. Pneumonia and otitis media are common complications; encephalitis is rare, and years after recovery some patients develop Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE), a progressive neurodegenerative disease with no cure. The infection is highly contagious, and public health measures are required promptly when a single case is detected. Transmission is via contact, underscoring the need for rapid isolation and response.

articles.headline: はしかの後に発病、SSPEは「社会で防ぐ」　重要なワクチン接種：朝日新聞
articles.headlineTranslated: SSPE Develops After Measles; "Preventable by Society" — The Importance of Vaccination: Asahi Shimbun
articles.summary: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) is a fatal, incurable brain disease that develops years after measles infection, now notably discussed in Japan. Measles outbreaks and vaccination history shape SSPE trends: 1975–1985 saw 13–27 annual cases; since 1986, declines followed by 1991–2000: 3–11; 2001–2006: 1–5; 2007–2012: 0–2. A 2022 national survey found 37 living SSPE patients with onset from 1983–2015; since 2017, no new cases confirmed. Exact incidence remains unclear. Diagnosis uses cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing; intrathecal interferon has been tried but no proven cure exists. Risk is highest when measles occurs before age 2, especially under age 1. Symptoms include cognitive decline, motor disturbance, myoclonus, and progressive loss of walking and speech, culminating in coma. Vaccination is the key preventive measure: routine one-dose at age 1 and a second dose in the year before entering elementary school; two doses confer strong protection and lessen transmission to unvaccinated infants.
